notes: 2025 volumes come from GIIGNL's Annual Report 2026 (exporter-by-importer matrix, with Kpler). Each leg groups the reported flows from one exporter to the destinations named. Where a country's exports are split across several of its plants (Australia's WA / Queensland / NT legs), the split is an estimate (marked ≈). Paths are illustrative routing through real ports and straits, not AIS tracks. 2026 run-rates are rough indications of current flow, not forecasts.

chokepoints.name: Strait of Hormuz
chokepoints.why: Every cargo from Qatar (14 trains at Ras Laffan) and the UAE's Das Island leaves through it, and there is no pipeline bypass for LNG. Oman's plant at Qalhat sits outside the strait, which is why it kept shipping in 2026.
chokepoints.status2026: Effectively closed to LNG since 28 Feb 2026. Qatar exported 1.6 Mt in September (a third to Kuwait, inside the Gulf) and Kpler expects ~0.6 Mt in October.
chokepoints.source: IEA Strait of Hormuz factsheet; EIA (Jul 2026); Kpler via Reuters/Cyprus Mail (12 Oct 2026)

chokepoints.name: Strait of Malacca / Singapore
chokepoints.why: The short way from the Gulf, Africa and the Atlantic into China, Korea and Japan. Most Qatari, Omani and Cape-routed Atlantic cargoes for North-East Asia pass here.
chokepoints.status2026: Open. Volumes through it fell with Qatar's outage.
chokepoints.source: EIA World Oil Transit Chokepoints; route estimates in this file

chokepoints.name: Bab-el-Mandeb
chokepoints.why: Southern gate of the Red Sea. Before 2024 roughly 8% of world LNG trade went through Bab-el-Mandeb and Suez, mostly Qatar to Europe. Since the Houthi attacks LNG carriers have almost entirely stopped using it.
chokepoints.status2026: Houthi attacks resumed in Feb 2026, they declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in July, and a Saudi-backed counter-offensive began on 4 Oct. LNG still goes round the Cape.
chokepoints.source: EIA; CNN (4 Oct 2026); Lloyd's List Intelligence

chokepoints.name: Suez Canal
chokepoints.why: Used to be the Qatar-to-Europe shortcut. It now mostly sees northbound-to-southbound cargoes for Egypt's floating import terminals (FSRUs) at Ain Sokhna, which are reached through the canal.
chokepoints.status2026: Open, but very few LNG transits to or from the Red Sea.

chokepoints.name: Cape of Good Hope
chokepoints.why: The detour for Middle East to Europe and for US Gulf to Asia cargoes that don't use Panama. It costs no canal fees, but Qatar to North-West Europe takes ~10–12 extra days, which ties up ships.
chokepoints.status2026: The default Europe-to-Asia LNG route for Atlantic cargoes and for the few Qatari cargoes heading west.

chokepoints.name: Panama Canal
chokepoints.why: Cuts a US Gulf to Japan voyage from about 35 days via the Cape to about 22–25 days. LNG carriers compete with container ships for scarce Neopanamax slots, and draught and slot limits bite in droughts.
chokepoints.status2026: El Niño drought: transits capped at 34 a day from 3 Sep, then 32 from 15 Sep, easing to 33 from 15 Oct. Laden LNG transits hit a two-year high in June as US cargoes chased Asian prices.
chokepoints.source: Panama Canal Authority; S&P Global (Jul 2026); Maritime Executive (Sep 2026)

chokepoints.name: Lombok / Makassar straits
chokepoints.why: The deep-water route north from Western Australia to Japan and Korea, bypassing Malacca entirely. That makes Australian LNG one of the most chokepoint-safe supplies in the world.

chokepoints.name: Northern Sea Route (Vilkitsky Strait)
chokepoints.why: The Arctic short cut from Yamal and Arctic LNG 2 to China. It is only navigable for conventional carriers from about July to November. In winter, Arc7 ice-breaking carriers go west to Europe, or trans-ship.
chokepoints.status2026: Summer season active. Arctic LNG 2's sanctioned cargoes go this way to Beihai, China.

chokepoints.name: Dardanelles / Turkish Straits
chokepoints.why: LNG for Turkey's Marmara Ereğlisi terminal (Algerian, US and Qatari cargoes). Daylight-only, one-way traffic rules apply.
chokepoints.source: BOTAŞ; route estimates in this file

legs.title: US Gulf Coast → France, Netherlands, UK, Spain, Germany…
legs.why: The biggest LNG flow in the world: 73.8 Mt in 2025, 58% of all European LNG. The US supplied 76% of Dutch and UK imports, 55% of Türkiye's and 45% of Spain's. US cargoes are mostly FOB at ~115% of Henry Hub plus a fixed liquefaction fee, so the offtaker sends each one wherever pays most after freight.
legs.statusText: Growing. US exports were up 23% in H1 2026, and the 2026 forecast is ~123 Mt (+14%). This is Europe's replacement for both Russian pipeline gas and Qatar's cargoes.

legs.title: US Gulf Coast → Japan, Korea, Taiwan (via Panama or Cape)
legs.why: Japan 4.7 Mt, South Korea 4.5 Mt and Taiwan 2.5 Mt in 2025. Almost no US LNG went to China in 2025 because of trade tensions (7% of China's supply in 2024, ~0 in 2025). Panama is the shortest way. It only pays when the JKM premium covers the extra freight plus the canal fee and the risk of waiting for a slot.
legs.statusText: In demand but constrained. Laden LNG transits hit a two-year high in June, then El Niño cut the canal to 32–33 transits a day. Slots are auctioned against container ships and LPG carriers (record $5.3m in Sep).

legs.title: US Gulf Coast → India, Thailand, Bangladesh (via Cape)
legs.why: India took 3.0 Mt of US LNG in 2025 (down 2.0 Mt) and US cargoes are its main source of flexibility. Thailand, Bangladesh and others took the rest. It is a long voyage round Africa that ties up far more of the fleet than a Europe run.
legs.statusText: Busier in 2026. South Asia lost most of its Qatari supply and bids for Atlantic cargoes, at prices it struggles to afford.

legs.title: US Gulf Coast → Brazil, Argentina, Caribbean
legs.why: Brazil (89% US-supplied), the Dominican Republic, Colombia, Puerto Rico, Chile, Argentina and Panama. Demand is weather-driven: imports jump in droughts when hydropower falls, and fell 17% in 2025 as rains returned. Most of it lands at floating terminals (FSRUs).
legs.statusText: Normal seasonal flow.

legs.title: US Gulf Coast → Egypt, Jordan, Kuwait (Middle East)
legs.why: Egypt went from exporter to major importer as its own gas output fell. Imports jumped from 2.5 Mt in 2024 to 9.2 Mt in 2025, 8.5 Mt of it from the US, landed through new FSRUs at Ain Sokhna (reached via the Suez Canal). The US supplied 56% of all Middle East and Africa LNG.
legs.statusText: Rising imports. Egypt now competes with Europe for Atlantic cargoes.

legs.title: Qatar → China, Taiwan, Korea, Japan, Thailand
legs.why: China 20.2 Mt, Taiwan 7.8, South Korea 7.3, Japan 3.4 and Thailand 2.1 in 2025. These are mostly long-term, oil-indexed contracts from the lowest-cost LNG in the world. Qatar supplied ~30% of China's LNG and was Taiwan's biggest supplier. Q-Flex and Q-Max carriers (up to 266,000 m³) were built for these runs.
legs.statusText: Largely halted. Force majeure since 2 Mar 2026 after Iranian strikes on Ras Laffan. Total Qatari exports were 1.6 Mt in Sep (under a quarter of normal), with ~0.6 Mt expected in Oct.
legs.source: GIIGNL Annual Report 2026; Kpler via Reuters (12 Oct 2026)

legs.title: Qatar → India, Pakistan, Bangladesh
legs.why: India 11.6 Mt, Pakistan 6.6 Mt (99% of its LNG) and Bangladesh ~4 Mt in 2025, on a voyage of only 3–5 days. Qatar and the UAE supplied 59% of India's LNG. These are the most Hormuz-exposed buyers in the world, and also the most price-sensitive.
legs.statusText: Largely halted. South Asian buyers are cutting gas-fired power and fertiliser output, or paying spot prices they struggle to afford.

legs.title: Qatar → Italy, Belgium, Poland, UK (via Cape since 2024)
legs.why: Italy 4.8 Mt (Adriatic LNG), Belgium 1.7 (Zeebrugge), Poland 1.6 and the UK 0.6 in 2025, only ~7% of Europe's LNG. Since early 2024 Qatari carriers avoid the Red Sea and sail round the Cape (dashed line = the old Suez route).
legs.statusText: Halted. Europe replaced the lost volume with US cargoes, which is one reason TTF more than doubled in Aug–Sep 2026.

legs.title: Qatar → Kuwait (inside the Gulf)
legs.why: Kuwait imported 6.8 Mt in 2025, 4.8 Mt of it from Qatar, at Al-Zour. It is a short run inside the Gulf that never needs to pass Hormuz.
legs.statusText: The one Qatari flow still moving. About a third of Qatar's September exports went to Kuwait, because those cargoes never have to cross Hormuz.
legs.source: GIIGNL Annual Report 2026; Kpler via Reuters (12 Oct 2026)

legs.title: UAE (Das Island) → India, Japan
legs.why: ADNOC's Das Island plant (5.8 Mtpa) inside the Gulf: India took 3.2 Mt and Japan 0.8 Mt in 2025. ADNOC's new 9.6 Mtpa Ruwais LNG (due 2028) is also inside Hormuz.
legs.statusText: Largely shut in behind Hormuz.

legs.title: Oman (Qalhat) → Japan, Korea, India, China, Taiwan
legs.why: Oman exported 11.5 Mt in 2025, 91% to Asia: Japan 3.0, India 2.1, South Korea 2.1, China 1.4 and Taiwan 1.1 Mt. Oman LNG at Qalhat sits on the Arabian Sea coast, outside Hormuz. Its 1 Mtpa Marsa LNG (2028) is at Sohar, also outside.
legs.statusText: Still flowing. Its cargoes earn a premium as the only Middle East LNG that avoids Hormuz.

legs.title: Western Australia → Japan, Korea, Taiwan
legs.why: Gorgon, Wheatstone, North West Shelf, Pluto and Prelude. Australia exported 78.8 Mt in 2025 and was Japan's (40%), China's (32%) and Korea's (32%) biggest supplier. The route runs through deep Indonesian straits with no Middle East or Malacca exposure. Country totals are from GIIGNL; the split across WA, Queensland and NT is an estimate.
legs.statusText: Unaffected and now highly valued. North West Shelf Train 2 was retired in 2025, and Pluto Train 2 (5 Mtpa) is due to start in 2026.
legs.source: GIIGNL Annual Report 2026; WA Govt LNG Profile (Jul 2026)

legs.title: Western Australia → China & South-East Asia
legs.why: China took 21.2 Mt of Australian LNG in 2025 (down 5.5 Mt), split between WA and Queensland. Western Australia on its own was 10% of global LNG exports.
legs.statusText: Unaffected.
legs.source: GIIGNL Annual Report 2026; WA Govt LNG Profile (Jul 2026); split estimated

legs.title: Queensland (Gladstone) → China, Japan, Korea
legs.why: Three coal-seam-gas plants on Curtis Island (QCLNG, APLNG, GLNG, ~25 Mtpa). From 2027 they must reserve 15–25% of gas for Australia's east coast under a new domestic reservation scheme.
legs.statusText: Unaffected.

legs.title: Northern Territory (Ichthys, Darwin) → Japan, Taiwan
legs.why: INPEX's Ichthys (8.9 Mtpa, offline 52 days in Aug–Oct 2025) and Darwin LNG, which loaded its first Barossa cargo in January 2026 after Bayu-Undan ran dry.
legs.statusText: Unaffected.

legs.title: Malaysia (Bintulu) → Japan, China, Korea, Taiwan
legs.why: Petronas's Bintulu complex plus floating units (32 Mtpa in total). In 2025 Japan took 33%, China 23% and South Korea 13%.
legs.statusText: Unaffected.

legs.title: Indonesia (Bontang, Tangguh) & Brunei → Korea, China, Japan
legs.why: Indonesia 15.9 Mt and Brunei 5.0 Mt in 2025. Indonesia is redirecting gas to its own market: Bontang runs only two trains, and the government asked producers to defer exports.
legs.statusText: Unaffected.

legs.title: PNG LNG → Japan, China, Taiwan
legs.why: ExxonMobil-led PNG LNG (8.3 Mtpa) ran above nameplate in 2025 after the Angore upstream project added gas. It delivered 1.8 Mt to Taiwan.
legs.statusText: Unaffected.

legs.title: Russia (Sakhalin-2) → Japan, China, Korea
legs.why: Sakhalin-2 (~10.8 Mtpa including small units) is only days from Japan, which took 5.7 Mt in 2025. China took 2.4 Mt and Korea 1.7 Mt. Output was largely unaffected by sanctions.
legs.statusText: Still flowing to Japan and China.

legs.title: Russia (Yamal LNG) → France, Belgium, Spain
legs.why: Yamal LNG (17.4 Mtpa) uses Arc7 ice-breaking carriers. Europe took ~75% of Yamal's 2025 volumes: France ~6.2 Mt, Belgium ~3.9 Mt, Spain ~2.8 Mt (17% of Spain's LNG). Trans-shipment in EU ports has been banned since March 2025, so cargoes are relayed at Murmansk.
legs.statusText: Still flowing for now. The EU bought a record 9.97 Mt from Yamal in H1 2026 (+16%). Short-term contracts have been banned since 25 Apr 2026, and all Russian LNG plus maritime services are banned from 1 Jan 2027.
legs.source: GIIGNL Annual Report 2026; Kpler via Reuters (Jul 2026); EU 19th sanctions package

legs.title: Russia (Yamal) → Asia (Northern Sea Route in summer)
legs.why: About 5 Mt of Yamal LNG went to Asia in 2025. The Arctic short cut is only navigable from about July to November, and the closed Red Sea route complicates winter voyages east.
legs.statusText: Seasonal. It will matter more from 2027 when the EU ban fully bites.

legs.title: Arctic LNG 2 → Beihai, China (sanctioned)
legs.why: Arctic LNG 2 (Train 1 6.6 Mtpa; Train 2 started May 2025) is crippled by US sanctions and a lack of ice-class ships. It delivered 1.3 Mt in 2025, all to China, mostly to the Beihai terminal via a 'shadow' fleet.
legs.statusText: Sanctioned but moving. Kpler assumes ~5.7 Mt in 2026 (about 45% utilisation of two trains) with no sanctions relief.

legs.title: Nigeria LNG → France, Türkiye, Spain, Portugal
legs.why: Bonny Island (22.2 Mtpa, six trains). Train 7 is over 80% complete and will lift it to 30 Mtpa. European-bound exports rose 2.3 Mt in 2025 as feed gas and pipeline security improved.
legs.statusText: Flowing. Atlantic supply that is free of chokepoints.

legs.title: Nigeria LNG → India, China, Japan (via Cape)
legs.why: West African cargoes swing between Europe and Asia on the JKM–TTF spread.
legs.statusText: Flowing.

legs.exporter: Angola, Congo, Eq. Guinea, Cameroon, Senegal/Mauritania
legs.title: Angola, Eq. Guinea, Cameroon, Mauritania, Congo → Europe & Asia
legs.why: Angola 4.9 Mt, Equatorial Guinea 2.8, Cameroon 1.4, Mauritania/Senegal 1.2 (GTA FLNG's first year) and Congo 0.7. Floating LNG is the growth story here: Congo's Nguya FLNG shipped its first cargo in Feb 2026, taking Congo to 3 Mtpa.
legs.statusText: Flowing.

legs.title: Algeria (Arzew, Skikda) → Türkiye, France, Italy, Spain
legs.why: Algeria was the world's first LNG exporter (Arzew, 1964) and has 25.3 Mtpa of capacity, but feed-gas shortages cut exports for a second year (−2.2 Mt in 2025). It supplied 27% of Türkiye's LNG.
legs.statusText: Flowing. Short-haul supply into a tight European market.

legs.title: Trinidad (Atlantic LNG) → Latin America, Europe, Asia
legs.why: Atlantic LNG (14.8 Mtpa nameplate) is feed-gas starved and Train 1 is shut. 2025 exports went to the Americas (3.3 Mt), Europe (1.9 Mt) and Asia (1.4 Mt). Shell's Aphrodite field adds gas from 2027.
legs.statusText: Flowing.

legs.title: Norway (Hammerfest) → NW Europe
legs.why: Equinor's Hammerfest/Snøhvit (4.2 Mtpa), Europe's only large LNG export plant. Output fell 40% in 2025 on a long planned shutdown.
legs.statusText: Flowing.

legs.title: LNG Canada (Kitimat) → Japan, Korea, China
legs.why: LNG Canada (14 Mtpa) started Train 1 in June 2025 and Train 2 in October. Its 2.0 Mt went to Korea (0.7), Japan (0.6), China (0.4) and Taiwan (0.3), about 10 days to Japan with no Panama Canal.
legs.statusText: Ramping up. Chokepoint-free supply arriving right when Asia needs it.

legs.title: Mozambique (Coral Sul FLNG) → Asia
legs.why: Eni's Coral South FLNG ran above nameplate (3.6 Mt): Korea 0.9, Thailand 0.7, India 0.6, Singapore 0.5. Coral Norte FLNG (3.6 Mtpa, 2028) and TotalEnergies' restarted 12.8 Mtpa Mozambique LNG follow.
legs.statusText: Flowing. More East African supply is coming later this decade.

legs.title: Peru LNG → Asia & Europe
legs.why: Hunt-led Peru LNG (4.45 Mtpa), South America's only LNG exporter. 2025 volumes went to Asia (2.0 Mt) and Europe (1.3 Mt).
legs.statusText: Flowing.

liquefaction.name: Sabine Pass
liquefaction.status: Operating; 6 trains, the largest US plant

liquefaction.name: Corpus Christi (incl. Stage 3)
liquefaction.status: 18 Mtpa incl. 4 Stage 3 midscale trains in service; 3 more due by end-2026; Trains 8–9 (3 Mtpa) under construction

liquefaction.name: Plaquemines
liquefaction.status: Phase 1 ~11 Mtpa; full project ~20 Mtpa by mid-2027 (FERC deadline Dec 2027); running at capacity

liquefaction.name: Golden Pass
liquefaction.status: Train 1 first cargo 22 Apr 2026; Train 2 H2 2026; Train 3 H1 2027

liquefaction.name: Ras Laffan (14 trains)
liquefaction.status: FORCE MAJEURE. Strikes on 2 Mar halted output; 18 Mar missiles damaged Trains 4 & 6 (−12.8 Mtpa, 3–5 yr repairs). North Field East first train now H1 2027

liquefaction.name: Bintulu MLNG
liquefaction.status: Malaysia total incl. floating units: 32 Mtpa

liquefaction.name: Bontang
liquefaction.status: Running well below its old 22 Mtpa peak

liquefaction.name: Arctic LNG 2
liquefaction.status: US-sanctioned. Train 1 (6.6 Mtpa) plus Train 2 from May 2025; 1.3 Mt shipped in 2025, all to China

liquefaction.name: Idku + Damietta
liquefaction.status: Mostly idle; Egypt is now a net importer

liquefaction.name: Congo FLNG
liquefaction.status: Tango FLNG 0.6 Mtpa + Nguya FLNG (first cargo Feb 2026) = 3 Mtpa

liquefaction.name: GTA FLNG
liquefaction.status: First cargo Apr 2025; ramped to ~3 Mtpa peak late 2025

liquefaction.name: Coral Sul FLNG
liquefaction.status: Operating; onshore Mozambique LNG (13 Mtpa) in construction

regas.name: Tokyo Bay terminals
regas.note: Japan: 65.9 Mt in 2025 (−0.5%), ~30 terminals. Suppliers: Australia 40%, Malaysia 15%, US 7%, Qatar 5%. Nuclear restarts and solar trimmed gas burn.

regas.name: Guangdong (Dapeng)
regas.note: China: 67.0 Mt in 2025 (−15%) as Russian pipeline gas (Power of Siberia at 38 bcm/yr) and domestic output grew. Regas capacity 173 Mtpa. Suppliers: Australia 32%, Qatar ~30%, Russia 11%, US ~0.

regas.name: Rudong / Shanghai
regas.note: East-coast hub for the Yangtze delta.

regas.name: Tianjin
regas.note: Serves winter heating demand around Beijing.

regas.name: Beihai
regas.note: Receives sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 cargoes since Aug 2025.

regas.name: Pyeongtaek / Incheon
regas.note: South Korea: 48.7 Mt in 2025 (+4%). Suppliers: Australia 32% (15.4 Mt), Malaysia 8.0, Qatar 7.3, US 4.5, Oman 2.0, Canada 0.7.

regas.name: Tongyeong
regas.note: KOGAS southern terminal.

regas.name: Yong-An (Kaohsiung) + Taichung
regas.note: Taiwan: 23.5 Mt in 2025 (+11%) after the nuclear phase-out (May 2025) and the new Guantang terminal. Qatar 7.8 Mt and Australia 7.8 Mt are the top suppliers. Island grid with only days of storage.
regas.capacitySource: LNG Prime (GIIGNL 2026 lists Taichung at 8 Mtpa after expansion)

regas.name: Dahej
regas.note: India: 25.3 Mt in 2025 (−6%). Qatar 11.6 Mt, UAE 3.2, US 3.0, Oman 2.1. 59% from behind Hormuz. Petronet's Dahej is among the largest single regas sites in the world.
regas.capacitySource: IGU World LNG Report 2026 via Swarajya (Jul 2026)

regas.name: Port Qasim FSRUs
regas.note: Pakistan: 6.7 Mt in 2025, 6.6 Mt of it Qatari: the most Hormuz-dependent LNG importer anywhere.

regas.name: Moheshkhali FSRUs
regas.note: Two FSRUs; frequent power-sector shortages when spot LNG is expensive.

regas.name: Map Ta Phut
regas.note: Thailand's domestic Gulf of Thailand gas is declining, so LNG imports keep rising.

regas.name: Singapore (Jurong)
regas.note: Import plus bunkering and re-export hub.

regas.name: Al-Zour
regas.note: Kuwait: 6.8 Mt in 2025, 4.8 Mt Qatari. It sits inside the Gulf, so in 2026 it is one of the few places Qatari cargoes can still reach.

regas.name: Isle of Grain
regas.note: UK: 9.6 Mt in 2025 (+21%), 76% from the US.

regas.name: Milford Haven (South Hook, Dragon)
regas.note: South Hook is part-owned by QatarEnergy and built for Q-Max carriers.

regas.name: Gate (Rotterdam) + Eemshaven
regas.note: Netherlands: 16.9 Mt in 2025 (+28%), 76% from the US. These are the TTF hub's main LNG entry points.

regas.name: Zeebrugge
regas.note: Belgium: 10.2 Mt in 2025 (+85%). Russia ~3.9 Mt, US 3.8, Qatar 1.7. Was the Yamal trans-shipment hub until the EU ban in Mar 2025.

regas.name: Dunkirk
regas.note: France: 22.8 Mt in 2025, Europe's largest LNG importer. US ~10.9 Mt, Russia ~6.2, Algeria 2.3. France has 4 onshore terminals plus Le Havre FSRU.

regas.name: Montoir-de-Bretagne
regas.note: Key European receiver of Yamal LNG.

regas.name: Fos (Cavaou, Tonkin)
regas.note: Mediterranean entry for southern France.

regas.name: Spanish terminals (Barcelona, Huelva, Cartagena…)
regas.note: Spain has 6–7 terminals, the largest regas fleet in Europe, but weak pipeline links north to France limit how much it can pass on.

regas.name: Huelva
regas.note: Atlantic-side Spanish terminal.

regas.name: Sines
regas.note: Portugal's only terminal; big Nigerian and US supply.

regas.name: Wilhelmshaven FSRUs
regas.note: Germany built its first LNG import terminal in under a year (Dec 2022) after losing Russian pipeline gas. It now has FSRUs at Wilhelmshaven, Brunsbüttel and Mukran.

regas.name: Brunsbüttel FSRU
regas.note: Elbe estuary.

regas.name: Mukran FSRU
regas.note: Baltic coast (Rügen).

regas.name: Świnoujście
regas.note: Poland's gateway, supplied by Qatar and the US.

regas.name: Klaipėda FSRU
regas.note: Named 'Independence': the Baltics' route away from Russian gas since 2014.

regas.name: Inkoo FSRU
regas.note: Finland/Baltics supply after the Balticconnector pipeline damage.

regas.name: Adriatic LNG (Rovigo)
regas.note: An offshore gravity-based structure, historically Qatar-supplied. Italy also has FSRUs at Ravenna, Livorno (OLT) and Panigaglia.

regas.name: Revithoussa + Alexandroupolis FSRU
regas.note: The gateway for US LNG into Bulgaria, the Balkans and (via the Vertical Corridor) Ukraine.

regas.name: Marmara Ereğlisi
regas.note: Türkiye: 12.0 Mt in 2025 (+32%). US 55%, Algeria 27%. 5+ terminals including FSRUs at Dörtyol and Saros.

regas.name: Ain Sokhna FSRUs
regas.note: Egypt: 9.2 Mt in 2025, up from 2.5 Mt, with 8.5 Mt from the US. It went from exporter to major importer in two years.

regas.name: Guanabara Bay FSRU
regas.note: Brazil imports in dry years when hydro is low.

regas.name: Escobar FSRU
regas.note: Winter-only imports; Argentina is building its own export FLNG on Vaca Muerta gas.

regas.name: Quintero
regas.note: Central Chile's power and industry supply.

regas.name: AES Andrés
regas.note: Caribbean hub; small-scale re-distribution.

importersSource: GIIGNL Annual Report 2026 (with Kpler): 2025 imports net of re-exports. 'All others' = the 427.9 Mt world total minus the 14 countries listed.

timeline.text: EU bans trans-shipment of Russian LNG in EU ports (Zeebrugge).
LNG Canada Trains 1 and 2 start: North America's first big Pacific export plant.
Record year: 427.9 Mt traded (+5.4%). US 109 Mt (+24). Europe +29% to 126 Mt, Asia −4%. China −15% to 67 Mt.
Darwin LNG restarts on Barossa gas; Congo's Nguya FLNG and Corpus Christi Stage 3 Train 5 start up.
US–Iran war closes the Strait of Hormuz. ~20% of global LNG supply sits behind it.
Iranian strikes hit Ras Laffan and Mesaieed. QatarEnergy halts LNG production and declares force majeure.
Missiles damage Ras Laffan Trains 4 and 6 (−12.8 Mtpa, 3–5 years to repair). EU bans new Russian gas contracts.
Golden Pass (Texas, 70% QatarEnergy) ships its first cargo. EU short-term Russian LNG ban starts 25 Apr.
Islamabad MoU briefly eases Hormuz but does not hold. Laden LNG transits through Panama hit a two-year high.
JKM front-month $21.45/MMBtu at end-July. EU took a record 9.97 Mt from Yamal in H1. Houthis declare a blockade on Saudi shipping.

Panama caps transits at 34, then 32 a day. Qatar ships 1.6 Mt (a third to Kuwait). 20 Sep: North Field East pushed to H1 2027. Late Sep: Asian and European LNG at highest since early 2023, ~3× pre-war.
A tanker is hit ~50 nm from Ras Laffan, and at least 18 ships are attacked around Hormuz in early October.
Kpler expects Qatari exports of only ~0.6 Mt this month.
Panama adds a Neopanamax slot (33 transits a day), still below normal.
EU ban on all Russian LNG imports and on maritime services to Russian LNG carriers takes effect.
Supply wave: North Field East (H1 start), Golden Pass T3, Plaquemines Phase 2, Rio Grande T1–3, CP2, Port Arthur T1.

Bloomberg, Qatar energy chief sees LNG expansion start-up in 2027 (20 Sep 2026)

Yamal/EU: Kpler via Reuters, Engineering News (13 Jul 2026); Urgewald
Panama Canal: S&P Global (Jul 2026), Maritime Executive, FreightWaves (Sep 2026)
UKMTO / FT reports on Hormuz attacks (Oct 2026)
Prices (indicative): lnginsights.com/prices, 5 Oct 2026; pre-crisis Asian spot $9–11/MMBtu per GIIGNL

events.title: LNG abandons the Red Sea
events.text: Houthi attacks pushed LNG carriers off the Suez/Bab-el-Mandeb route (~8% of world LNG before 2024). Attacks resumed in Feb 2026, and a Tihamah strike in Bab-el-Mandeb killed 6 on 11 Aug 2026.

events.title: LNG Canada first cargo
events.text: Train 1 started June 2025 and Train 2 in October: the first big North American Pacific plant.

events.title: Arctic LNG 2 → Beihai
events.text: The sanctioned plant shipped 1.3 Mt in 2025, all to China, mostly via a shadow fleet into Beihai.

events.title: Plaquemines at full capacity
events.text: Venture Global's Plaquemines drove most of the +24 Mt US growth in 2025.

events.title: Darwin restarts on Barossa
events.text: First Barossa LNG cargo from Darwin LNG.

events.title: Hormuz closes
events.text: The US–Iran war closes the strait: ~20% of world LNG supply (Qatar + UAE) sits behind it.

events.title: Ras Laffan + Mesaieed hit
events.text: Iranian strikes: QatarEnergy halts all LNG production and declares force majeure.

events.title: Trains 4 & 6 damaged
events.text: Missiles damage Ras Laffan LNG Trains 4 and 6: −12.8 Mtpa (~16% of Qatar's 2025 exports), repairs 3–5 years. One Pearl GTL train is also hit.

events.title: EU bans short-term Russian LNG
events.text: New Russian contracts banned since 18 Mar. Yet EU imports from Yamal hit a record 9.97 Mt in H1 2026. Full ban from 1 Jan 2027.

events.title: Golden Pass first cargo
events.text: The 18 Mtpa Texas plant, 70% owned by QatarEnergy, starts up just as Qatar's own exports stop.

events.title: Panama: LNG transits 2-yr high
events.text: US cargoes chase Asian prices after Qatar's outage.

events.title: Panama caps: 34 → 32 a day
events.text: El Niño drought: first daily transit cap since 2023–24 (normal ~36), easing to 33 from 15 Oct.

events.title: Qatar ships 1.6 Mt: a third to Kuwait
events.text: Under a quarter of normal. Kuwait's Al-Zour terminal is reachable without crossing Hormuz.

events.title: North Field East slips to H1 2027
events.text: Qatar's minister: first NFE train in H1 2027, others during 2027. Equipment deliveries are hit by the Hormuz crisis.

events.title: Tanker hit near Ras Laffan
events.text: The tanker Acers was hit by projectiles ~50 nm north of Madinat ash Shamal.

events.title: ≥18 ships attacked in Hormuz
events.text: The FT counted ≥18 vessels attacked 1–11 Oct, with more on 11 and 13 Oct. LNG carriers cross with AIS switched off.

events.title: Qatar: ~0.6 Mt expected
events.text: Kpler expects Qatari LNG exports of only ~0.6 Mt in October (pre-war ≈6.7 Mt a month).
